Value-dependent wording and claims

Source: vignettes/wording.Rmd
wording.Rmd

This article is for authors whose sentences depend on the data: a count that may be one or many, a trend that may rise or fall, a statement that is only true above a threshold. After it you will be able to let a value choose its own wording, check what a sentence asserts with claim(), and list every wording a document can produce before the data arrive.

Spans

A span is a bracket of prose followed by an attribute block that holds a governor key: n, list, if or sign. The key’s value is an R expression, in double quotes. The bracket holds one or more arms, separated by |. The governor’s value chooses one arm, and only that arm prints.

[a site | # sites]{n="n_sites"}

Inside an arm, # stands for the governor’s value as printed. Arms are trimmed, so spaces around | do not matter.

Key The value must be Arms Chosen
n a single number 1 always (a template for #)
2 one / other
3 zero / one / other
4 zero / one / two / other
list a vector of any length 2 one / other
3 zero / one / other
4 zero / one / two / other
if one or more conditions, each TRUE or FALSE 2 true / false
1 always (a guard)
sign a single number 2 positive / negative
3 positive / negative / zero

A wrong number of arms for the key is a construct error, found from the source before anything runs.

The examples in this article come from one document. Its data chunk is:

n_sites <- 1
n_lost <- 0
n_visits <- 3
flagged <- c("Upper", "Lower")
none_flagged <- character(0)
slope <- 0.31
d_abund <- -0.042
d_cover <- 0
depth <- 2.46
mod <- data.frame(rising = c(TRUE, TRUE, TRUE))
n_missing <- 0
core <- 1
trend <- weft::brk(. < 0.95 ~ "a fall in", . <= 1.05 ~ "no change in",
                   TRUE ~ "a rise in")
ratio <- 1.12

Counts: n

An n span chooses a plural form.

We visited [a site | # sites]{n="n_sites"}.

[No samples were | One sample was | # samples were]{n="n_lost"} lost.

The logger was cleaned [never | once | twice | # times]{n="n_visits"}.
We visited a site.

No samples were lost.

The logger was cleaned 3 times.

The span sees the value as it prints. The “one” arm is chosen only when the number prints as exactly “1”, so a value printed with decimals takes the “other” arm:

The core was [# metre | # metres]{n="core"} long, or
[# metre | # metres]{n="core" digits="1"}.
The core was 1 metre long, or 1.0 metres.

Formatter classes and the keys digits and sigfig on an n or sign span format the number that # prints. With none, .num formats it.

An n governor must be one number. A vector is an error that tells you to count it:

v <- c("Upper", "Lower")
weft_str('[a site | # sites]{n="v"}')
#> Error:
#> ! weft: chunk unnamed-chunk-6: An `n` governor must be a single number, not a vector; write `length(x)` to count the elements of a vector (rule 1.5.11)

Lists: list

A list span chooses its arm by the length of a vector, and # prints the vector joined with “and”. Use it when a list can be empty:

[No sites were | # was | # were]{list="flagged"} flagged.

[No sites were | # was | # were]{list="none_flagged"} flagged.
Upper and Lower were flagged.

No sites were flagged.

A list class on the span, such as .or, changes how # joins the items. A vector that holds an NA, or a value that is not a vector at all (a data frame, NULL), is a missing value, so a misspelt column cannot print “No sites were flagged”.

Conditions: if

An if span with two arms chooses between them. Its value is one or more conditions separated by commas, and all must be TRUE for the first arm.

Phosphorus [rose | fell]{if="slope > 0"} over the period.
Phosphorus rose over the period.

An empty second arm makes optional text. Write the empty arm with a space before the closing bracket:

Sampling was complete[, apart from the estuary sites | ]{if="n_missing > 0"}.
Sampling was complete.

When an arm prints nothing, weft removes one space beside it, so you write ordinary spacing around the span.

Guards

An if span with one arm is a guard. It always prints its words, and it fails the render when a condition is not TRUE. Wrap the word that makes the claim:

[All]{if="all(mod$rising)"} `r nrow(mod)` models rise.
All 3 models rise.

If one model stops rising, the sentence is false. Here is a short document, guard.Rmd, with that data and an empty list:

```{r data}
mod <- data.frame(rising = c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE))
flagged <- character(0)
```

[All]{if="all(mod$rising)"} `r nrow(mod)` models rise.

[# was | # were]{list="flagged"} flagged.

Its render fails with:

weft: 2 claims failed
  guard.Rmd:14  "All"
      all(mod$rising) was FALSE
      optional text is written [phrase | ]{if="…"}
  guard.Rmd:16  "# was"
      the list is empty, and a two-arm `list` span has no arm for the empty case (rule 1.5.3); add a first arm for the empty case
      add a first arm for the empty case
Read each sentence. If FALSE is right, rewrite the sentence.
Do not loosen a claim to clear this.

The second failure in that report is another case with no arm: a two-arm list span given an empty vector. A two-arm sign span at zero is one too. weft treats each as a failed claim, because no wording was written for it.

Direction: sign

A sign span chooses by the sign of a number. # prints the size without its sign, so the arm carries the direction:

Abundance [rose by # | fell by # | did not change]{.pct sign="d_abund"}.

Cover [rose by # | fell by # | did not change]{.pct sign="d_cover"}.
Abundance fell by 4.2%.

Cover did not change.

A sign span judges zero on the number as printed: a change that prints as “0.0%” takes the zero arm.

d <- -0.0004
weft_str("Cover [rose by # | fell by # | did not change]{.pct sign=\"d\"}.")
#> [1] "Cover did not change."

Agreement

Whole arms are the plain way to make words agree. An inner span can also follow the enclosing count with n=".":

[# sample[ | s]{n="."} [was | were]{n="."} taken]{n="n_sites"}.

`r flagged`{.and} [was | were]{n="length(flagged)"} sampled.
1 sample was taken.

Upper and Lower were sampled.

A value or a span can carry an id, written #name in its attribute block. A later span refers to it with n="#name", and agrees with the value as it printed there, without evaluating it again:

Depth was `r depth`{#d .num} m, and the [core was | cores were]{n="#d"} kept.
Depth was 2.5 m, and the cores were kept.

The id must be defined earlier in the same document.

Writing | and # in an arm

A doubled || or ## in an arm is a literal | or #. A backslash before either is removed first, so \| also works, and inside a pipe-table cell the separator itself must be written \|.

weft_str('[a||b | c]{if="TRUE"}')
#> [1] "a|b"

Checks: claim()

claim(x, check, ...) returns x unchanged after checking it. In a check, . stands for x. Each check is a separate argument and is reported on its own.

claim(5, . > 1)
#> [1] 5
claim(c(3, 4), sum(.) == 7, all(. > 0))
#> [1] 3 4

Use claim() inside a value, so the render fails when the sentence around it stops being true: `r claim(n_exceed, . >= 10)`. It works inside a larger expression too, as in `r trend(claim(ratio, . > 0))`, and in a governor: [a site | # sites]{n="claim(k, . > 0)"}.

Where the check runs decides what happens when it fails:

  • In inline R during a knit (prose, a caption, a weft_str() string), the failure is collected and the render fails at the end with the full report.
  • Everywhere else (chunk code, a targets pipeline, the console), it stops at once with an error of class weft_claim_failed.
n_exceed <- 7
claim(n_exceed, . >= 10)
#> Error:
#> ! weft: 1 failed claim
#>   check `. >= 10` failed (value: 7)

A check written with level = "warn" never fails. In a knit the value prints as if the check passed, and the check is listed at the end of the knit:

Gauges that fell: `r claim(n_down, . >= 10, level = "warn")` in all.
weft: 1 warned check(s)
  extra.Rmd:18  `r claim(n_down, . >= 10, level = "warn")`
      . >= 10 was FALSE (value 7)

Outside a knit it is an R warning:

claim(7, . >= 10, level = "warn")
#> Warning: weft: check `. >= 10` failed (value: 7)
#> [1] 7

claim(x) with no check is an error, and so is a check with no variable in it, such as claim(x, TRUE): the lint inert-check finds it.

When a check fails, the report asks you to read the sentence. Either the sentence, the check or the data is wrong. Loosening the check until it passes hides a sentence that is no longer true.

Phrases chosen by key or by range

lookup() builds a function that turns a key into a phrase. brk() builds one that turns a number into a phrase by ranges, tried in order:

tier_lab <- lookup(c(ref = "Reference", mod = "Moderately disturbed"))
tier_lab("mod")
#> [1] "Moderately disturbed"
trend <- brk(. < 0.95 ~ "a fall in", . <= 1.05 ~ "no change in",
             TRUE ~ "a rise in")
trend(c(0.9, 1, 1.12))
#> [1] "a fall in"    "no change in" "a rise in"

In prose the call is an ordinary value:

The index showed `r trend(ratio)` abundance.
The index showed a rise in abundance.

Both functions stop on a key or a value they cannot place, and an NA is a “no value” failure: it never falls through to a default phrase.

tier_lab("high")
#> Error:
#> ! lookup(): "high" is not a key; the keys are "ref", "mod" (rule 3.3.2).
trend(NA)
#> Error:
#> ! A brk() function was given a missing value (NA, NaN, Inf, -Inf or a value of length zero).

A lookup() or brk() that a project uses in more than one place belongs in the dictionary, as a labels or breaks entry (see vignette("units", package = "weft")).

Phrase functions

Some wording is fixed by arithmetic. These functions print it:

of_n(3, 7, "site", "sites")
#> <weft_text>
#> [1] "3 of the 7 sites"
of_n(0, 4, "site", "sites")
#> <weft_text>
#> [1] "none of the 4 sites"
of_n(1, 1, "site", "sites")
#> <weft_text>
#> [1] "the only site"
of_n(2, 2, "site", "sites")
#> <weft_text>
#> [1] "both sites"
of_n(5, 5, "site", "sites")
#> <weft_text>
#> [1] "all 5 sites"
about(0.48)
#> <weft_text>
#> [1] "nearly half"
about(0.52)
#> <weft_text>
#> [1] "just over half"
about(0.32, to = 1/3)
#> <weft_text>
#> [1] "nearly a third"
ci(2.1, 1.3, 2.9)
#> <weft_text>
#> [1] "2.1 (95% CI 1.3 to 2.9)"
pm(2.1, 0.3)
#> <weft_text>
#> [1] "2.1 ± 0.3"
clamp(0.004, floor = 0.01)
#> <weft_text>
#> [1] "< 0.01"

about() refuses a value that is further than its tolerance from the target, because “nearly half” would then be false:

about(0.3)
#> Error:
#> ! about(0.3, to = 0.5): the value is further than the tolerance (0.05) from the target, so "half" would not be true.

weft_setup() does not put these functions on the search path. In a document, write weft::of_n(), or call library(weft) in a chunk.

The tolerance of about() and the level of ci() come from the settings about_tolerance (0.05) and ci_level (0.95).

Spans in R code

plural() is the function form of an n span:

plural(1, "a person", "# people")
#> [1] "a person"
plural(0, "never", "once", "twice", "# times")
#> [1] "never"

if and sign spans have no function form. In R code an if is R’s own, and a sign span is written as markup in a weft_str() string.

Numbers from a source

A number quoted from another study is not computed, so it goes in a cite span. The span prints its words and, with an @, the citation:

Earlier work found [0.5 m in the upper reach]{cite="@doe2019"}.
Earlier work found 0.5 m in the upper reach (Doe 2019).

With a bare key, cite="doe2019", the span prints only its words, and you write the citation elsewhere in the same paragraph. Each key must be in the bibliography: weft checks this at knit time and in the lints.

A fixed number with no source, such as a method’s filter size, is marked with the class .weft-literal and a why that records the reason:

Samples were filtered through
[0.45 µm]{.weft-literal why="pore size set by the laboratory method"} membranes.
Samples were filtered through 0.45 µm membranes.

The why is removed from the output. Both marks exempt the number from the numeral lint (see vignette("lints", package = "weft")).

Every wording a document can produce

A document that renders on new data each day can say things nobody has read yet. weft gives two tools to see them in advance.

arms() reads a document, runs no R, and lists every arm of every span:

f <- file.path(tempdir(), "daily.Rmd")
writeLines(c(
  "---",
  "title: \"Daily turbidity\"",
  "output: md_document",
  "params:",
  "  readings: [4.2, 7.9, 12.6]",
  "knitr:",
  "  opts_knit:",
  "    weft: !expr weft::weft_setup()",
  "---",
  "",
  "```{r data}",
  "x <- unlist(params$readings)",
  "n_high <- sum(x > 10)",
  "change <- x[length(x)] - x[1]",
  "```",
  "",
  "[No gauge | One gauge | # gauges]{n=\"n_high\"} read above 10 NTU today.",
  "Turbidity [rose by # | fell by # | did not change]{sign=\"change\"} NTU over the day."
), f)
arms(f)
#> daily.Rmd:17  n="n_high"
#>   1 (zero)  No gauge
#>   2 (one)  One gauge
#>   3 (other)  # gauges
#> daily.Rmd:18  sign="change"
#>   1 (positive)  rose by #
#>   2 (negative)  fell by #
#>   3 (zero)  did not change

rehearse() knits the document once for each case, a named list of params, each in a fresh R process, and reports which arm each span chose and which arms no case reached. It writes nothing to the project.

rehearse("daily.Rmd", cases = list(
  usual = list(),
  calm  = list(readings = c(3.1, 3.4, 3.1)),
  storm = list(readings = c(11.2, 14.8, 30.5))
))
case usual: ok
  arms chosen:
    daily.Rmd:17  n="n_high"  arm 2 (one)  One gauge
    daily.Rmd:18  sign="change"  arm 1 (positive)  rose by #
case calm: ok
  arms chosen:
    daily.Rmd:17  n="n_high"  arm 1 (zero)  No gauge
    daily.Rmd:18  sign="change"  arm 3 (zero)  did not change
case storm: ok
  arms chosen:
    daily.Rmd:17  n="n_high"  arm 3 (other)  # gauges
    daily.Rmd:18  sign="change"  arm 1 (positive)  rose by #

1 arm that no case reached:
  daily.Rmd:18  sign="change"  arm 2 (negative)  fell by #
Every span was evaluated by some case.

No case made turbidity fall over the day, so “fell by #” has never been rendered. Add a case that does, and read the sentence it produces. rehearse() changes only params: a document that reads its data some other way renders the same data in every case.
